key: We have accepted thousands from Dhvasra’s and Purusanti’s hands: Swift runs this giver of delight.
s: Near the close of a short hymn to Soma, the singers turn to gifts received; Sāyaṇa, on 9.58.3, takes the givers as kings whose large gift weighed on two seers like swallowed poison, until this hymn they saw made it count as taken, not accepted.

evidence.words: ध्वस्रः कश्चिद्राजा पुरुषन्तिः कश्चित् । तयोरुभयोः । अत्र इतरेतरयोगविवक्षया द्विवचनं द्रष्टव्यम् । “सहस्राणि धनानां सहस्राणि “आ “दद्महे वयं प्रतिगृह्णीमः । तदस्माभिः प्रतिगृहीतं धनमुत्तममस्त्विति ऋषिः सोमं प्रार्थयत इति सोमस्य स्तुतिः । सिद्धमन्यत् । यथावत्सार एतयोर्धनानि प्रतिजग्राह एवं तरन्तपुरुमीळ्हौ प्रतिजगृहतुः । तथा च शाट्यायनकम्--- ‘ अथ ह वै तरन्त पुरुमीळ्हौ वैददश्वी ध्वस्रयोः पुरुषन्त्योर्बहु प्रतिगृह्य गरगिराविव मेनाते तौ ह स्माङ्गुल्या सातं प्रतिममृशाते तावकामयेतामसातं नाविवेदं सातं स्यादात्तमिवैव न प्रतिगृहीतमिति तावेतञ्चतुर्ऋचमपश्यतां तेन प्रत्यैतां ततो वै तयोरसातं सातमभवदात्तमिवैव न प्रतिगृहीतं
evidence.gloss: Dhvasra is a certain king, Puruṣanti a certain other; of those two. Thousands of riches we accept. The seer prays Soma that the wealth we accepted be excellent: so it is praise of Soma. As Avatsāra accepted these two’s riches, so did Taranta and Purumīḷha; and so the Śāṭyāyanaka: Taranta and Purumīḷha, sons of Vidadaśva, having accepted much (bahu pratigṛhya) from Dhvasra and Puruṣanti, thought themselves like swallowers of poison (garagirāv iva menāte); they touched the gain with a finger and wished that this gain be no gain to them, as though merely taken, not accepted as a gift. They saw this four-verse hymn (etaṃ caturṛcam apaśyatām) and by it went back; then their gain became no gain, as though merely taken, not accepted (āttam ivaiva na pratigṛhītam).

reason: The critic holds on both counts. day.js: 9.58 has four verses, and the key is verse 3, the first of the two on the gifts, so “Closing” became “Near the close of a short hymn to Soma”. Re-opened packet.js veda 96 --verse 9.58.3: Sāyaṇa glosses Dhvasra as a king and cites the Śāṭyāyanaka: the two seers, bahu pratigṛhya garagirāv iva menāte (having accepted much, thought themselves swallowers of poison), saw this four-verse hymn (etaṃ caturṛcam apaśyatām), and their gain became āttam ivaiva na pratigṛhītam (as though taken, not accepted as a gift). The sentence now gives that point, with “takes the givers as kings” still governing.
